window_text:
[5] Sophia: Hi. My name is Sophia Dominguez. And I'm the CEO and co-founder of SVRF. Imagine a world where you don't need your phone or a computer. Where visuals just appear in front of your eyes. Information and content flows through you, seamlessly, around you, at all times. The need for screens ends because rectangles are no longer as important. The future of this content is happening already, and everything I just described is not something that I've just made up; it's happening today on our phones already, and it's only going to get better. So that leads me to what we're focusing on today. Okay. I totally messed up.
[6] Jillian: That's okay Not a problem.
[7] Phil: You can start again if you want.
[8] Sophia: Okay.
[9] Phil: Start again. That's fine.
Right off the bat, Sophia’s nerves get the better of her. But she resets… and starts again.
[10] Sophia: We're no longer confined to a rectangle or to a screen. Holograms appear in front of you. Stories unfold all around you.
[11] Jillian: Slow it down.
[12] Sophia: This is no longer sci-fi. We can do everything I just described on our phones and it's only going to get better. The type of content that works in this new realm we call immersive content. We define it as 360 degree photos and videos, 3D objects and environments, 3D masks, filters and lenses. And the creation of this content is growing exponentially. Search engines evolve out of every new content type. We've seen this in the past with websites, with Google, products and images with Pinterest, videos with YouTube and GIFs with Giphy. Immersive content will be no different
So it sounds like Sophia wants to build the equivalent of Google for this new type of content: immersive content. And apparently there’s tons of it out there already. But there’s no easy way to find it.
[13] Sophia: And thus we started SVRF.
[14] Phil: So can you explain it a little bit? If we take a step back where is this immersive content now? How are we currently using it? And then how's it going to grow?
[15] Sophia: Yeah. So we index today about 23 different sites. So there's different ways in which they'll be indexed. We look for a very specific type of file, and these file types range from anything from JPEG, PNG, MP4
[16] Michael: I'm sorry, I'm totally confused. What exactly are we doing? SVRF does what? Let's start again.
[17] Howie: Yeah. Are you a search engine?
[18] Sophia: Yes.
[19] Howie: Okay.
[20] Michael: So I go to SVRF dot - you have a URL - and I go to that to do what?
[21] Sophia: Yes. So you can search for all immersive content. But that's actually not what we're focused on today So what we realized is that most media consumption happens on social networks, such as Snapchat and Instagram
[22] Michael: Stop there. Instagram. We all use Instagram. What do you do?
[23] Sophia: Okay. So I'm sure you've seen that there are face masks and other elements that are immersive content that are layered on top of people.
[24] Michael: Like Snapchat put bunny faces on?
[25] Howie: Yeah, they’re starting to do that on Instagram.
[26] Sophia: Yes. So that is a type of immersive content.
[27] Michael: Okay.
[28] Sophia: So utilizing the camera suddenly you have a bunny face or a dog face. That is one type of immersive content. There’s other types of immersive content which you see which companies like Apple which are doing Animoji stuff. So suddenly you turn yourself into a character
[29] Jillian: I have. Yes.
[30] Sophia: Yeah. And it’s becoming very consumer and very normal behavior. But the next generation of that is to also allow you to be anywhere at the same time. So you’re a panda, but it’s still kind of weird that you’re in this podcast studio. But I could then search utilizing our API to be like, I want to be in a jungle. And so suddenly you’re a panda that’s literally in a jungle just through the camera. And so we’re enabling that search database.
You’ve probably used these filters before. You’ve thrown on a dog face or a voice changer with Snapchat … But maybe you haven't been thinking about this the way Sophia is: as augmented reality, virtual reality's less intimidating cousin. And that's a big part of what SVRF is all about ...
[31] Michael: So help us old folks with something here. Why are we doing this? What's going on here?
[32] Phil: For me to be a panda in another dimension?
[33] Jillian: You don't have to be a panda.
[34] Michael: You are always a panda in another dimension.
[35] Sophia: You don't have to be. That was one example.
[36] Jillian: Okay. So you're just walking into other... Realities.
[37] Sophia: There's different levels of immersive content.
[38] Michael: Did you invent that technology that did that? Or what did you do?
[39] Sophia: The content. So we powered the content. So today we've been porting our experiences to Snapchat. So we take some sort of asset and then build it into Snapchat's Lens Studio and then promote it on Snapchat. What we want to do and what we're focused on now is building this API that automatically would just do the conversion process and then be able to power this content very seamlessly into companies like Snapchat, Instagram
[40] Howie: So Apple, Instagram, Snapchat, they're already doing this. I can turn myself into a panda. I don't think I can turn myself into a panda in the jungle. But are you selling your API to Instagram?
[41] Sophia: Not selling. But we're partnership with all camera-enabled companies. So any sort of social AR and VR company that's looking for more content.
[42] Howie: Give me an example.
[43] Sophia: So for example today we’re partner with this company called Metaverse. And so what they allow is you can very easily build AR experiences. And so we provide them with a database of content that allows their users to like more readily build these types of experiences.
[44] Howie: Is it a licensing type of deal? I mean, you said a partnership. What does a partnership mean?
[45] Sophia: They integrated our API.
[46] Michael: How are you going to generate revenue? How is it going to be a business? How is it an investable asset?
[47] Sophia: Yeah. So what we’re focused on right... We today power 1.25 million experiences across our applications.
[48] Michael: Per?
[49] Sophia: Per month.
[50] Michael: Okay.
[51] Jillian: And what does that mean in revenue?
[52] Sophia: So we’re currently not generating any revenue. And we want to grow to 50 million experiences per month, mostly through the API partnerships, and then monetizing through the API
[53] Phil: When you get to 50 million experiences a month, how do you monetize?
[54] Sophia: what we want to do is do sponsored posts from within the API. So instead of just focusing around people coming to SVRF.com, utilizing the API as a way to get more eyeballs, and essentially have sponsored posts there. So for example, if I'm Nike, we create some sort of experience, they want to pay for premier placement of anyone who's searching through sports or whatever the experience is about, then they get prime placement
[55] Phil: So you have to get to, you feel like you have to get to 50 million experiences a month and then you'll have enough scale to be interesting to brands.
[56] Sophia: Yes.
[57] Phil: What kind of revenue can you generate from that?
[58] Sophia: M-hm. I mean, it's really honestly unknown We're still figuring it out But I think for us it's about how do we get to 50 million? And how do we get that scale. And also in the meantime work with the brands
[59] Howie: Sponsored posts are the only source of monetization? Can't you come up with some kind of licensing fee or something that can... If you're going to really be behind the scenes powering all this stuff, can't you charge for that?
[60] Phil: Like in other words, wouldn't Instagram pay you a licensing fee to use this?
[61] Sophia: Mm, I don't think that they would. Partly because Giphy has been the only company to kind of break through and be able to partner with Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat, all these different places. And they have specifically chosen not to charge these companies, because for them it's about scale and distribution. And I think that we'll follow a similar path
Sophia's modeling her business on Giphy, which could be really smart. So let's talk about Giphy for a second..
You might have used GIPHY without even knowing it. If you’ve sent a GIF on Twitter, or via text on an iPhone, then it was likely through their their custom integration or API.
It’s been reported that GIPHY has 300 million active users …
every day
. So if Sophia can achieve something similar in the AR/VR space, that kind of scale could really turn investors’ heads.
[62] Michael: Just tell us what this is. This is purely a bet that you can scale to have a tremendous amount of usage. And the idea is that you sell this business to someone who wants that line of traffic. Right? That's what this is? I mean, you clearly have no want to really to make revenue. You're on a... Which is maybe sometimes not a - I can't believe I'm saying this - but in this game, this is what you're doing. You just want crazy traffic and then you want to flip the business, right?
[63] Sophia: No. I wouldn't say that at all. I think that we do want crazy traffic. And I think we want to power all this content. But I think focusing too early on that will not allow us to focus on scale. And how do we get as many partnerships as possible and reach. And therefore turning that around and turning it into an actual business.
[64] Jillian: I like this. I really like you
[65] Sophia: Thank you
[66] Jillian: What does this look like in three years? What do you want it to be? What does success look like?
[67] Sophia: So success looks like we are the company... I think like ten years down the line.
[68] Jillian: Okay. I’ll go ten.
[69] Sophia: What we think about is we are the company that owns the glasses or the contacts that basically power reality distortion. Because that’s what we actually want to do. Because if you say, I want to suddenly be at the beach somewhere, the company that powers that is also the company that actually has the device that does that.
[70] Jillian: That’s interesting.
[71] Phil: So you want to be eventually in the hardware business?
[72] Sophia: Eventually.
[73] Jillian: Would that be being acquired by a hardware? Because that’s really capital intense.
[74] Sophia: Yeah. I mean I think it’s a long way away.
[75] Jillian: But I like the moon shot. I look at companies that have a moon shot and an earth shot. That’s the moon shot. That’s really cool Give me the earth shot.
[76] Sophia: Within three years, if we’re integrated with every social application and basically powering their entire database of lenses and we’re the known brand for immersive content, period
[77] Michael: So who is 'we' and what's your secret sauce?
[78] Sophia: mhm so I've been passionate about augmented reality and virtual reality forever And I'm a product person. So I had one other company before. umm [00:15:23] We sort of turned it into a dating app. But we decided that we didn't want to work on a dating app and so we shut it down. But in during my time there, that's when I started AllThingsVR, which was one of the first virtual reality newsletters, and trying to help people understand what was happening in the virtual reality and augmented reality industries. And generated this idea of SVRF, realizing that there's going to be increasingly amounts of content there needs to be someone to organize it and allow people to surface it in various applications
[79] Michael: What valuation are you raising at now this round again?
[80] Sophia: Seven million.
[81] Jillian: And your last was...?
[82] Sophia: Three
[83] Phil: The previous round.
[84] Sophia: A little over a year ago.
[85] Howie: How do you have money?
[86] Sophia: So we’ve raised $730,000 so far.
[87] Jillian: And what are you doing now?
[88] Sophia: Right now we're raising 1.5
[89] Phil: If I were going to invest in this space, I would absolutely invest in you.
[90] Sophia: Thank you.
[91] Phil: But this is not a space... It’s not even so much the space that I don’t like. It’s just it’s so early and We don’t know how much revenue you can generate from sponsored posts. You’re a long way from getting to the scale that you need to even approach these brands. And frankly, it also concerns, your long-term vision for the company concerns me when you start talking about getting into the hardware space. I don’t want to invest in a hardware company. I like the search engine business. And the API business. I don’t want to be in the hardware business. And so that long-term vision doesn’t align with what I would look for in an investment. So I’m going to pass.
Phil is out. But there are 3 investors who’d like to learn more. Including Jillian.
[92] Jillian: What’s the biggest pushback on this from....
[93] Sophia: Market timing.
[94] Jillian: Okay. Keep going.
[95] Sophia: So originally when I started pitching this, ummm we really focused on AR and VR. But got passes within six seconds of somebody looking at the document because it literally only said AR and VR. And what we are really focused on is not necessarily headsets at all People were saying that headsets growth is going to be huge. And we were like, that’s not going to happen. Nobody really wants to wear a headset. But this content is so interesting. How can we make this content interesting for the people of today And that’s where Snapchat and places like Instagram and these sort of lenses and filters really come in handy, because it’s just so natural to see this content and experience this content through the camera. And realizing that early has set us ahead.
[96] Howie: I think it's interesting that you are shying away from the AR/VR conversation. Because you got some pushback. I know that VR was very heavily hyped a few years ago Then the bottom fell out. AR seems to be more on the path with some market viability.
[97] Sophia: Yeah. It's just, VR is in a nuclear winter and AR is in a very cold times.
[98] Howie: Right. Which to me is, okay, there’s going to be AR and VR in our life at some point. So this is a great time to invest in this type of sector. can you talk about any of the exciting things of how this content could be practically applied or implemented through AR/VR? Do you have partnerships on that?
[99] Sophia: Yeah. So I think the thing... The area where I’m most interested is everything that Apple is doing and also Samsung is doing with these characters. And we’ve seen this with companies like Snapchat and Bitmoji and then with Apple with Animoji. And I think another reason why companies [00:31:00] like Apple, they’re focusing on how do we mask how somebody looks? Because the number one reason why people don’t video chat is because they don’t like the way that they look, so if you can change that, that allows more and more people to share video, to talk on video, etc, etc. And I think it’s just it’s a more natural way to communicate than just being on the phone.
[100] Howie: Not to call you out, but it's funny that you said it's a more natural way to communicate if we turn ourselves into animals.
[101] Jillian: Well, look at what happened with gaming.
[102] Michael: I caught that. I'm like...
[103] Howie: That is the new normal.
[104] Michael: Maybe there is a differential in the age thing. Like I call Phil, hey Phil, I’m a panda. I’m in a forest.
[105] Phil: You’re a panda today. Cool!
[106] Howie: I want to be a dragon.
[107] Michael: Let's talk about that deal. I'm a lion.
[108] Jillian: I want to be a dragon! That's what I want to be.
[109] Michael: But do you know, I laugh, but people do it. They love it. They love it. I mean, I laughed at Snapchat and everybody's a princess and a bunny-eyed thing and I don't know what's going on. But I think you do it once, it's funny. Twice, I couldn't stand it Look, I like you a lot. I think you answered our questions really well. I think you're very smart and I think you're a product person at the core. I think you like what you're doing. I think you're passionate about what you're doing. All those things make you a good entrepreneur. Umm I think for now I’m out. You know, it's funny, I got to tell you, I am a little on the fence here. Because I actually think you do have something. I just don't know how to gauge it
Michael is out. Here’s Howie
[110] Howie: With this, I don't know how big the upside is I usually like to swim in the post-seed waters; probably the round that would be coming after this. Just to really be able to evaluate more, have more metrics to really understand how people are engaging, are they re-engaging, I like, I really like you, [00:38:00] I like this. And I say to myself, if when I was getting... If I were to get pitched, if Snapchat pitched to me seven years ago, I would have passed, because I didn't get it. And I'd be kicking myself for passing. Right? Because I would have just been like oh, that's just a stupid app. It's a generational thing. I didn't realize what it was going to be and this paradigm shift that was happening. I don't want to miss the boat on this, because I feel like there's something really special here. So I do want to keep in touch. And then if you need to raise more money in your next round as you ramp up to Series A, I'd love to have that conversation.
[111] Sophia: Awesome. Cool. Appreciate that.
[112] Howie: Yeah
With Howie’s pass, that makes Jillian the last investor left.
[113] Jillian: I think you are... You’re sharp. You know every single... You have an answer, a smart answer to every question. You know your stuff. You’re confident. There’s just so much here. I love the fact that you went out and you started this newsletter. So you’re a pioneer. And that’s fantastic. I want to put 50 into this round. I might put in more, to tell you the truth. But I really do want to speak to some of the other investors, if you’re open to that?
[114] Sophia: Of course.
[115] Jillian: But I’m going to commit 50 now, So I’m in!
decision_quote: But I’m going to commit 50 now, So I’m in!

taxonomy.label: business_model_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the startup’s revenue model, monetization approach, or service/automation mix as a driver of business viability.

taxonomy.label: business_viability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's concern that the overall business viability, model, or economics are not sufficiently compelling.

taxonomy.label: capital_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the startup will require substantial ongoing capital investment, increasing risk or misalignment with the investor’s funding capacity.

taxonomy.label: competitive_advantage_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s beliefs about what drives defensibility or sustainable competitive advantage in a market.

taxonomy.label: competitive_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the category is highly competitive, attention‐constrained, and requires heavy marketing to win, reducing the likelihood of outsized success.

taxonomy.label: competitive_landscape_inertia
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the difficulty of displacing or changing behavior of incumbents due to entrenched solutions, habits, or workflows.

taxonomy.label: deal_terms_complexity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the structure or details of deal terms (e.g., convertibles, SAFEs, preferred terms) may introduce complexity, ambiguity, or unfavorable outcomes.

taxonomy.label: decision_context_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints imposed by the specific evaluation format, environment, or context rather than the startup's fundamentals.

taxonomy.label: dilution_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the financing plan will cause excessive dilution relative to their ownership goals or stage fit.

taxonomy.label: execution_risk_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the team may not yet have demonstrated sufficient execution reliability or maturity for the risk level of the round.

taxonomy.label: founder_equity_incentive_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to ensuring founders retain sufficient ownership to remain properly motivated, aligned, and incentivized for the long-term company‐building journey.

taxonomy.label: founder_execution
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of the founders' execution ability, resourcefulness, pace, and operational grit.

taxonomy.label: founder_market_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales based on how well the founder's background, experience, or motivation aligns with the target market.

taxonomy.label: founder_qualities
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the founders' personal traits, capabilities, or appeal.

taxonomy.label: founder_skillset
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the founder's core skills or functional strengths relevant to company-building.

taxonomy.label: fund_economics_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor’s fund size, check size, or ownership goals that constrain how selective they must be when choosing investments.

taxonomy.label: fundraising_demand_signal
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the company will attract capital easily due to current or expected investor demand.

taxonomy.label: growth_projection_risk
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the company’s growth, revenue, or user‐scale projections are insufficiently modeled, unrealistic, or lack credible underlying assumptions.

taxonomy.label: investment_thesis_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's predefined investment thesis or mandate that restricts them to specific sectors, business models, or company types.

taxonomy.label: investment_upside_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's view that the risk‐reward profile offers disproportionately large potential returns relative to downside risk.

taxonomy.label: investor_domain_knowledge_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor lacking the necessary domain knowledge to effectively assess the technology, moat, competition, or overall viability of the opportunity.

taxonomy.label: investor_experience_bias
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's prior personal experiences, wins, losses, or operational history that shape their judgment of a new opportunity.

taxonomy.label: market_entry_path_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that there is a clear, reachable initial customer segment that can serve as an effective wedge into the larger market.

taxonomy.label: market_problem_validation
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor perceiving the underlying problem as real, important, or painful enough to support a venture-scale solution.

taxonomy.label: market_size_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s belief about the absolute or relative size and fluidity of the addressable market.

taxonomy.label: market_timing
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the timing is favorable or unfavorable for this market, category, or product to emerge or scale.

taxonomy.label: mission_alignment_preference
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's personal or emotional alignment with the startup's mission or purpose.

taxonomy.label: portfolio_conflict_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints arising from existing portfolio investments that create competitive conflicts preventing a new investment.

taxonomy.label: product_adoption
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to evidence that end users are adopting and using the product meaningfully.

taxonomy.label: product_appeal_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s positive perception of the product’s appeal, quality, or desirability based on their own reaction.

taxonomy.label: product_differentiation_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to how unique, defensible, or hard-to-copy the product or technology is perceived to be.

taxonomy.label: product_success_factor_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to which product components or attributes are perceived as most essential to the startup's ability to succeed.

taxonomy.label: solution_feasibility_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the proposed product or solution is technically or operationally feasible.

taxonomy.label: stage_valuation_mismatch
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of a mismatch between the company’s stage of progress and the valuation being requested.

taxonomy.label: traction_repeatability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that current traction, usage, or revenue signals are too early or insufficiently repeatable to support scaling.

taxonomy.label: unit_economics_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the business benefits from structurally attractive unit economics, such as profitable or self-reinforcing customer acquisition.

taxonomy.label: venture_scale_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the companys market dynamics, ceiling, or competitive landscape limit its ability to achieve venture-scale outcomes.

taxonomy.label: investor_value_add_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the investor can contribute meaningful help, networks, or domain value beyond capital to this specific company.

taxonomy.label: founder_coachability_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how receptive the founder is to feedback, advice, or course-correction and their ability to read and respond to the room.

taxonomy.label: founder_communication_quality
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the founder's clarity, articulation, command of their numbers, and storytelling ability when presenting the business.

taxonomy.label: founder_motivation_authenticity
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the genuineness, personal connection, or origin of the founder's drive to work on this particular problem.

taxonomy.label: go_to_market_strategy_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how the company will reach and acquire customers, including sales motion, channel scalability, and cost of acquisition.

taxonomy.label: founder_investor_vision_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the founder's intended direction or focus for the company aligns with the path the investor believes in or would back.

taxonomy.label: corporate_structure_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the company's legal entity, incorporation, jurisdiction, or IP-ownership structure as a barrier or condition to investing.
